title: How GPS actually knows where you are

scenes.text: Your phone finds you without ever sending a signal to a satellite.
scenes.claim: GPS receivers only listen to satellite broadcasts; they do not transmit to the satellites.

scenes.text: About thirty satellites orbit twenty thousand kilometres up, each broadcasting the time from an atomic clock.
scenes.claim: The GPS constellation has roughly thirty satellites at about 20,200 km altitude carrying atomic clocks.

scenes.text: Your phone measures how long each signal took to arrive. Multiply by the speed of light, and you have a distance.
scenes.claim: Distance to a satellite equals signal travel time multiplied by the speed of light.

scenes.text: One distance puts you on a giant sphere. Three spheres meet at just two points, and one is out in space.
scenes.claim: Intersecting three spheres gives two candidate points; one is typically far from Earth's surface.

scenes.text: A fourth satellite corrects your phone's cheap clock, because one billionth of a second is thirty centimetres of error.
scenes.claim: Light travels about 30 cm in one nanosecond, so a 1 ns clock error is about 30 cm of range error.

scenes.text: Relativity is built in. Without its corrections, GPS would drift by about ten kilometres every day.
scenes.claim: Uncorrected relativistic clock offsets of roughly 38 microseconds per day would cause errors of about 10 km per day.

scenes.text: Every time a map finds you, it quietly proves Einstein right.
scenes.claim: GPS timing depends on relativistic corrections that match general and special relativity.
